Click so that I don't have to touch the camera to take the picture or if I'm on my keyboard and I want to speak to text. I would do not want to have to try to find the button to speech to text. turns.response_html:
This is a great question, and you are definitely not alone in wanting hands-free, touch-free ways to control your phone. Finding tiny buttons (like the speech-to-text mic) can be frustrating, and touching the screen while trying to set up a camera shot is often inconvenient.

Because you are using an Android device, you actually have quite a few highly customizable tools built right into your phone's operating system to accomplish exactly what you are asking for.

Here is how you can set up external clickers, use mouth/facial movements, and execute screen taps without touching the glass.

1. Using an External Clicker (Switch Access)

Android has a built-in accessibility tool called Switch Access that is designed specifically for this.

  • How it works: You can buy a cheap Bluetooth button or clicker (often sold as camera remotes or accessibility switches) and pair it with your phone. Instead of just acting as a volume button, you can configure the clicker to "tap" the screen, select items, or act as a universal selection tool.
  • How to set it up: Go to Settings > Accessibility > Switch Access. From there, you can connect your Bluetooth device and assign exactly what you want the "click" to do.

2. Using Mouth Movements (Camera Switches)

If you want to use your mouth to trigger a tap without needing to hold a physical device, Android offers a brilliant feature called Camera Switches.

  • How it works: Rather than listening for the sound of a tongue click, your phone uses the front-facing camera to look for specific facial gestures. You can map gestures to screen taps. For example, you can set it so that every time you open your mouth, smile, or raise your eyebrows, the phone will register a screen tap or trigger a specific action.
  • How to set it up: Go to Settings > Accessibility > Switch Access > Settings > Camera Switches.

3. Tapping Anywhere on the Screen via Voice (Voice Access)

To solve your issue of accidentally hitting the wrong buttons when trying to find the tiny Speech-to-Text icon, you should try Voice Access.

  • How it works: Voice Access allows you to navigate your entire phone completely hands-free. You can simply say, "Tap microphone" or "Tap camera."
  • The "Grid" Feature: If you want to tap a highly specific, random location on your screen without touching it, you can simply say, "Show grid." Your phone will overlay a numbered grid across the entire screen. You just say the number out loud (e.g., "Seven"), and the phone will immediately tap that exact spot for you.
  • How to set it up: Go to Settings > Accessibility > Voice Access (If it's not there, you can download the official Google "Voice Access" app for free from the Play Store).

4. Clapping Hands or Custom Noises (Third-Party Apps)

Currently, Android's native settings do not listen for non-verbal audio triggers like a hand clap or a tongue click (it relies on the camera for facial gestures or the microphone for spoken words). However, you can easily achieve this with third-party automation apps!

  • MacroDroid or Tasker: These are incredibly popular Android automation apps available on the Play Store. You can easily build a "Macro" (a mini-program) that tells your phone: "If the microphone detects a sudden loud noise (like clapping hands), then simulate a screen tap on the center of the screen."

5. Quick Camera Hacks

If your main goal is getting a camera shot without touching the phone, check your native Camera app settings for Shooting Methods. Most modern Androids (like Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel phones) have built-in toggles that let you:

  • Take a picture by simply saying "Smile," "Cheese," or "Capture."
  • Take a picture by simply holding your open palm up to the camera (the phone will see your hand, start a 3-second timer, and snap the photo).

Recommendation to start: I highly recommend trying Voice Access first, specifically for the "Show Grid" command. It takes exactly the frustration out of finding tiny buttons that you are describing!

turns.response_html:
As a software engineer and hardware enthusiast, you’re hitting on the classic "build vs. buy" dilemma. While you could dive into Developer Options or even root the device to build a custom listener, there are actually more efficient ways to handle this that bridge the gap between native tools and full DIY hardware.

Since you're already familiar with things like KiCad and 3D printing (and you've got that 90 alpha TPU for a nice tactile button), you have a few sophisticated routes to explore.

1. The "Native" Path: Sound Switches

Android’s Switch Access has a feature specifically for non-verbal sounds. It’s significantly more intuitive than the "Show Grid" command because it uses short, distinct audio triggers instead of natural language processing.

  • How it works: You can map specific sounds—like a tongue click ("T" or "K" sound) or a "pop"—to specific actions, such as "Select" or "Next."
  • Location: Settings > Accessibility > Switch Access > Settings > Camera Switches / Sound Switches.
  • Battery Impact: It does use the microphone, but it's generally lighter than full Voice Access because it’s looking for simple waveforms rather than transcribing speech. However, for a marathon runner like you who might be out for hours, any constant mic usage is a non-zero drain.

2. The Engineer’s Path: DIY Bluetooth HID (BLE)

Given your background in PCB design and hardware, this is likely your most rewarding and "intuitive" route. You can bypass the touchscreen and the microphone entirely.

  • The Concept: Build a small ESP32-based (or Nordic-based) Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) device that acts as a standard HID (Human Interface Device).
  • Why this is better: A BLE clicker consumes almost zero battery on your phone. You can program the ESP32 to send a "Volume Up" or a specific "Media Key" signal, which many apps (like the Camera) already treat as a shutter button.
  • Customization: If you want it to hit a specific coordinate (like the speech-to-text mic), you can use an automation app (see below) to "listen" for that specific Bluetooth button press and execute a shell command to tap x, y.
  • Hardware Project: You could design a tiny PCB in KiCad, 3D print a rugged housing, and have a "clicker" that clips to your gear or fits in your palm.

3. The "Jailbreak" Alternative: Tasker + Shell Commands

You mentioned using Developer Tools. If you enable USB Debugging (or Wireless Debugging), you can use an automation powerhouse like Tasker combined with a plugin called AutoInput.

  • The Workflow: You set a "Profile" in Tasker that triggers when it detects a specific sound (via a plugin) or a specific hardware button press.
  • The Action: Instead of a cumbersome menu, Tasker executes a shell command: input tap <x> <y>.
  • The "Developer" Edge: Since you understand shell scripts (being a Fish shell and Neovim user), you can write logic that says: "If Camera app is open, tap the shutter coordinates; if Keyboard is open, tap the mic coordinates."

My Recommendation

If you want the lowest battery drain and the most intuitive feel: Go the Hardware HID route. Use an ESP32 to send a "Enter" or "Volume" key over Bluetooth. Then, use Tasker to intercept that keypress and translate it into a screen tap at a specific coordinate. It’s a "set it and forget it" solution that doesn't keep your microphone active.

Since you’re comfortable with Developer Tools and ADB, you can actually build a much more "elegant" and context-aware system than the standard accessibility menus.

Because you're a software engineer who likes DIY hardware (and presumably prefers low-level control over heavy GUI apps), you can treat your phone like a terminal and your audio triggers as scripts.

1. The "Engineer's Logic" for App-Specific Actions

You don't need the phone to "know" everything all the time. You can create a conditional logic gate using Tasker (the gold standard for Android automation) or Automate.

The Logic Flow:

  1. Trigger: An incoming signal (Bluetooth clicker or a Sound Trigger).
  2. Check Context: IF (Foreground App == "com.android.camera").
  3. Action: adb shell input tap <shutter_x> <shutter_y>.
  4. Else IF: (Foreground App == "com.keyboard.app").
  5. Action: adb shell input tap <mic_x> <mic_y>.
  6. Else: Launch "Voice Access" or show a custom menu.

2. Implementation: Hardware vs. Sound

Option A: The DIY BLE Clicker (Recommended)

Since you do PCB design (KiCad) and 3D printing, this is the most "pro" route.

  • The Hardware: Build a tiny clicker using an ESP32-C3 (which has built-in BLE).
  • The Code: Program it as a Bluetooth HID Keyboard. Have it send a rare keycode (like F10) when clicked.
  • The Phone Side: Use Tasker. Set an "Event" for "Any Key" or use a plugin like AutoInput to detect that F10.
  • Why this wins: Zero microphone battery drain. It’s "instant-on." You can 3D print a custom housing with a satisfying tactile switch for your camera rig.

Option B: Low-Level Sound Triggers (No DIY Hardware)

If you want to stick to sounds (tongue clicks), use the Android Sound Trigger HAL.

  • Native Tool: Go to Settings > Accessibility > Switch Access > Sound Switches.
  • The Bridge: Map a "Tongue Click" to a specific "Key Press" (like Volume Up).
  • The Logic: Use Tasker to intercept that Volume Up event. Tasker can differentiate between a physical volume press and one generated by the accessibility service.
  • Context Control: Inside Tasker, add a "Profile Constraint" for the "App" (e.g., Camera). This ensures that a tongue click only triggers a photo when the camera is actually open.

3. Precision "Tapping" via Developer Tools

To find the exact coordinates for your input tap commands:

  1. Enable Developer Options.
  2. Turn on Pointer Location.
  3. Tap exactly where the shutter button or the mic icon is. You’ll see the X and Y coordinates at the top of your screen.
  4. Hardcode these into your Tasker script or your adb shell commands.

4. Handling the "Home Menu" Navigation

To make the Home Screen "intuitive" without high battery drain:

  • Set a Tasker profile where, if the Foreground App is "Launcher" (your home screen), your audio trigger opens a "Scene."
  • In Tasker, a "Scene" is a custom-designed overlay. You can make it a simple menu with giant buttons for "Messages," "Music," etc., which can then be navigated via the same clicker/sound.

Engineer-to-Engineer Tip: If you find the microphone drain is an issue, look into MacroDroid. It has a specific trigger for "Media Button Pressed" that works exceptionally well with cheap $5 Bluetooth camera shutters. You can buy one, take the PCB out, and integrate it into a 3D-printed tool that fits your workflow perfectly.

Using your Garmin watch is a brilliant "hacker" solution. Since it’s already bonded via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), you can leverage it as a remote trigger without the battery drain or "always-listening" privacy concerns of a microphone-based system.

Because you have a background in software engineering and are already building your own LifeOS, you can implement this using a "bridge" approach that gives you full control over your phone’s screen.

1. The "Tasker + Connect IQ" Bridge

This is the most direct way to turn your watch buttons into screen taps.

  • On the Watch: Install a Connect IQ app like "Tasker Trigger" or "Garmin Tasker." These apps allow you to assign specific watch buttons (or menu items) to send a signal to your phone.
  • On the Phone: Use Tasker combined with the AutoNotification plugin. When you press the button on your watch, the Connect IQ app sends a notification to your phone. Tasker intercepts that notification and runs a script.

2. Executing the "Tap" (The Developer Tool Method)

To make this intuitive and context-aware (so it only taps the shutter button when the Camera is open), use a Shell command in Tasker.

Step A: Find your Coordinates

  1. Go to Settings > Developer Options.
  2. Enable Pointer Location.
  3. Open your Camera and tap the shutter button; note the X and Y coordinates at the top of the screen. Do the same for the keyboard's microphone icon.

Step B: The Tasker Script Create a Tasker profile that triggers on the watch button press. Inside the task, use the Run Shell action:

# If Camera is open, tap the shutter
input tap 540 1850 

# If Keyboard is open, tap the mic
input tap 950 1200

Note: You can use Tasker's %WIN (Window title) or "App Context" to ensure the tap only happens in the right app.

3. The "LifeOS" Integration (The SDK Route)

Since you are comfortable with PCB design and software dev, you might prefer a more custom, non-app-store solution.

  • Garmin Mobile SDK: You can build a small "Listener" app for Android using the Garmin Connect IQ Mobile SDK. This allows your phone to listen for specific "Messages" sent from a custom-coded watch widget (written in Monkey C).
  • Why this is better: You can bypass the "notification" method entirely. Your watch can send a raw data packet to your phone, which your LifeOS "server" (running on the phone) intercepts to trigger an ADB command.

4. Battery and Performance

  • BLE Efficiency: Since Garmin watches use Bluetooth Low Energy and are designed for 24/7 connection, the impact on your phone's battery is negligible compared to keeping the microphone active for Voice Access.
  • No "Always-On" Mic: This setup is completely silent and only "wakes up" the processing logic the millisecond you click the watch button.

Since you already have the vivoactive 5, you have a perfect low-power "bridge" device. Because it is already connected via Bluetooth, you can use it as a remote trigger for ADB-style shell commands on your phone without the battery drain of an active microphone.

The most efficient way to achieve this—giving you specific taps for the camera, speech-to-text, and home navigation—is to create a pipeline using Tasker and a Connect IQ bridge.

1. The Setup (The "Hacker" Pipeline)

To get a button on your watch to trigger a specific tap on your phone, you need three pieces of software working together:

  1. On the Watch: Install the Tasker Trigger or Garmin Tasker app from the Connect IQ store.
  2. On the Phone: Install Tasker and the AutoNotification plugin.
  3. The Logic: The watch app sends a "message" to your phone; AutoNotification intercepts it; Tasker executes the screen tap.

2. Precise Coordinates (Developer Tools)

To make sure the "click" hits the exact right spot (like that tiny speech-to-text mic), use the coordinates from your phone’s system:

  • Go to Settings > Developer Options.
  • Enable Pointer Location.
  • Open your keyboard and tap the microphone icon. Note the X and Y coordinates displayed at the top of the screen (e.g., X: 950, Y: 1240).

3. Context-Aware Logic

You can set Tasker to behave differently depending on which app you are currently using. In Tasker, create a Profile with two conditions:

  1. State: AutoNotification Intercept (from your Garmin).
  2. App: Camera (or Keyboard/Messaging).

The Task Script: Inside the task, use the Run Shell action. This uses the same logic as adb shell but runs locally on the device:

  • For Camera: input tap [shutter_x] [shutter_y]
  • For Keyboard: input tap [mic_x] [mic_y]
  • For Home Screen: If no specific app is open, you can set the trigger to run a command like input keyevent 3 (Home) or launch Voice Access automatically.

4. Native Alternatives (Out-of-the-Box)

If you want to skip the manual coordinate setup for the camera specifically, there are dedicated apps for the vivoactive 5 that interact directly with the Android camera API:

  • CameraClick: This Connect IQ app allows you to use the watch screen as a shutter button for your native phone camera. It handles the "tap" logic internally.
  • Music Controls Hack: On many Android phones, the "Volume Up" button acts as a camera shutter. You can often use the default Music Provider on your Garmin to "Increase Volume," which will trigger the camera shutter if the app is open.

Why this works for your setup:

  • Battery: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) stays connected anyway for your notifications, so the "cost" of sending a trigger is nearly zero.
  • Reliability: Physical buttons (or a dedicated watch face tap) are more reliable than "listening" for a clap in a noisy environment.
  • Privacy: No microphone is "always on" or processing audio data.

If you want to go deeper into the automation, Tasker can also be configured to only "listen" for these watch triggers when certain conditions are met (like when your phone is plugged into a tripod or at specific GPS coordinates), making it truly intuitive without cluttering your normal phone use.
